title: Der Sperling und seine vier Kinder
titleEn: The Sparrow and His Four Children
part: The Sparrow and His Four Children
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 157. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). 1857 spelling preserved exactly (daß, thu, thut).
about: KHM 157 is less a fairy tale than a fable with a sermon attached: an old sparrow, uneasy that his four fledglings scattered into the world without any of his warnings, finds them again in the autumn and questions each in turn about how he has managed and what dangers — cats, snares, hunters — he has learned to dodge. The fourth son answers with piety rather than cunning, and the tale closes with a rhymed moral about trusting providence over one's own cleverness; expect the tone to feel closer to Aesop or a devotional tract than to Grimm's usual magic.

sentences.t: Ein Sperling hatte vier Junge in einem Schwalbennest.
sentences.l: A sparrow had four young in a swallow’s nest.
sentences.n: “Junge” (young ones, nestlings) is a neuter plural noun here. Sperling = sparrow; the nest is a swallow’s, not his own.

sentences.t: Wie sie nun flück sind, stoßen böse Buben das Nest ein, sie kommen aber alle glücklich in Windbraus davon.
sentences.l: When they are now fledged, wicked boys knock the nest in; but they all get away happily in a gust of wind.
sentences.i: Just as they are fledged, wicked boys smash the nest in — but they all escape safely in a rush of wind.
sentences.n: “flück” is an older/dialectal form of flügge, fledged, able to fly. “Windbraus” = a roaring gust of wind; “davonkommen” = to get away, escape. The narrative present (“stoßen … kommen”) is normal in these tales.

sentences.t: Nun ist dem Alten leid, weil seine Söhne in die Welt kommen, daß er sie nicht vor allerlei Gefahr erst verwarnet, und ihnen gute Lehren fürgesagt habe.
sentences.l: Now the old one is sorry, because his sons go out into the world, that he has not first warned them of all sorts of danger, and told them good lessons beforehand.
sentences.i: Now the old one is grieved that, with his sons going out into the world, he has not first warned them against every kind of danger and set out good counsel for them.
sentences.n: “dem Alten ist leid” — a dative of the person: “to the old one it is sorry,” i.e. he regrets. “verwarnet” and “fürgesagt” are older forms (modern verwarnt, vorgesagt); “für-” here = vor-, beforehand.

sentences.t: Aufn Herbst kommen in einem Weizenacker viel Sperlinge zusammen, allda trifft der Alte seine vier Jungen an, die führt er voll Freuden mit sich heim.
sentences.l: Towards autumn many sparrows come together in a wheat-field; there the old one meets his four young, and leads them, full of joy, home with him.
sentences.i: When autumn comes, many sparrows gather in a wheat-field; there the old one comes upon his four young, and leads them home with him, full of joy.
sentences.n: “Aufn” = auf den (towards, at the coming of); “allda” = da/dort, there (archaic). “antreffen” = to come upon, encounter — the separable “an” sits at the clause end.

sentences.t: „Ach, meine lieben Söhne, was habt ihr mir den Sommer über Sorge gemacht, dieweil ihr ohne meine Lehre in Winde kamet; höret meine Worte und folget eurem Vater und sehet euch wohl vor: kleine Vöglein haben große Gefährlichkeit auszustehen!“
sentences.l: “Ah, my dear sons, what worry you have made me the summer through, since you came into the winds without my teaching; hear my words and follow your father and look well to yourselves: little birds have great perils to endure!”
sentences.i: “Ah, my dear sons, what worry you have caused me all summer long, since you went off into the winds without my teaching; hear my words, and heed your father, and be well on your guard: little birds have great dangers to withstand!”
sentences.n: “den Sommer über” = all summer long (an accusative of duration around “über”). “dieweil” = weil/während, since/while (archaic). “höret, folget, sehet … vor” are old plural imperatives in -et; “sich vorsehen” = to be on one’s guard. “kamet” = kamt, you came.

sentences.t: darauf fragte er den ältern wo er sich den Sommer über aufgehalten und wie er sich ernähret hätte.
sentences.l: thereupon he asked the elder where he had kept himself the summer through and how he had fed himself.
sentences.i: thereupon he asked the elder where he had spent the summer and how he had fed himself.
sentences.n: “sich aufhalten” = to stay, dwell; “sich ernähren” = to feed oneself, make a living. “ernähret … hätte” is the subjunctive of the reported question, “how he had fed himself.”

sentences.t: „Ich habe mich in den Gärten gehalten, Räuplein und Würmlein gesucht, bis die Kirschen reif wurden.“
sentences.l: “I have kept to the gardens, sought little caterpillars and little worms, until the cherries grew ripe.”
sentences.i: “I kept to the gardens and looked for little caterpillars and worms until the cherries ripened.”
sentences.n: “Räuplein” and “Würmlein” are diminutives (Räupchen/Würmchen), little caterpillars and worms — the -lein ending recurs all through this tale. “sich halten in” = to keep to, stay in.

sentences.t: „Ach, mein Sohn,“ sagte der Vater, „die Schnabelweid ist nicht bös, aber es ist große Gefahr dabei, darum habe fortan deiner wohl Acht, und sonderlich wenn Leut in Gärten umher gehn, die lange grüne Stangen tragen, die inwendig hohl sind und oben ein Löchlein haben.“
sentences.l: “Ah, my son,” said the father, “the beak-pasture is not bad, but there is great danger in it; so from now on take good heed of yourself, and especially when people go about in gardens carrying long green poles that are hollow inside and have a little hole at the top.”
sentences.i: “Ah, my son,” said the father, “the feeding is not bad, but there is great danger with it; so from now on keep good watch over yourself, and above all when people walk about in gardens carrying long green poles, hollow inside and with a little hole at the top.”
sentences.n: “Schnabelweid(e)” = literally “beak-pasture,” the birds’ feeding-ground. “deiner wohl Acht haben” — “Acht haben” (take heed) governs the genitive “deiner,” heed of yourself. The green poles are blowpipes; “Leut” = Leute, people (the shared gloss carries a Bavarian tag, but the sense — people — is right here).

sentences.t: „Ja, mein Vater, wenn dann ein grün Blättlein aufs Löchlein mit Wachs geklebt wäre?“ spricht der Sohn.
sentences.l: “Yes, my father, but what if a little green leaf were stuck over the little hole with wax?” says the son.
sentences.i: “Yes, father — but what if a little green leaf were stuck over the hole with wax?” says the son.
sentences.n: The son imagines a blowpipe made harmless. “grün Blättlein” — the uninflected “grün” (for grünes) is old poetic usage. “aufs” = auf das; “spricht” (says) is the storyteller’s present.

sentences.t: „Wo hast du das gesehen?“
sentences.l: “Where have you seen that?”
sentences.n: The father’s recurring probe — he puts the same question to each son after their clever answers. Plain perfect tense.

sentences.t: „In eines Kaufmanns Garten“ sagte der Junge.
sentences.l: “In a merchant’s garden,” said the young one.
sentences.n: “eines Kaufmanns” is genitive — “of a merchant,” a merchant’s. “der Junge” = the young one, the young bird.

sentences.t: „O mein Sohn,“ spricht der Vater, „Kaufleut, geschwinde Leut!
sentences.l: “O my son,” says the father, “merchants — quick folk!
sentences.i: “O my son,” says the father, “merchants are sharp folk!
sentences.n: The father talks in clipped proverbs. “Kaufleut” = Kaufleute, merchants; “geschwinde Leut” = quick, nimble people — sharp dealers. The exclamation runs straight on into the next sentence.

sentences.t: bist du um die Weltkinder gewesen, so hast du Weltgeschmeidigkeit genug gelernt, siehe und brauchs nur recht wohl und trau dir nicht zu viel.“
sentences.l: if you have been about the children of the world, then you have learned worldly suppleness enough; only see and use it rightly well, and do not trust yourself too much.”
sentences.i: if you have been among the children of the world, then you have learned worldly cunning enough; only see that you use it rightly, and do not trust yourself too far.”
sentences.n: “bist du … gewesen, so …” — a conditional without “wenn,” marked by verb-first word order: “(if) you have been …, then …” “Weltkinder” = worldly people; “Weltgeschmeidigkeit” = worldly pliancy, sharpness. “brauchs” = brauche es, use it.

sentences.t: Darauf befragt er den andern „wo hast du dein Wesen gehabt?“
sentences.l: Thereupon he asks the second one, “where have you had your being?”
sentences.i: Thereupon he asks the second, “where have you made your home?”
sentences.n: “der andere” here = the second of the four. “sein Wesen haben” = to have one’s dwelling, be at home somewhere.

sentences.t: „Zu Hofe“ spricht der Sohn.
sentences.l: “At court,” says the son.
sentences.n: “zu Hofe” = an einem Hof / bei Hofe, at a (great) court — the dative with old -e ending. This son has lived around a noble household.

sentences.t: „Sperling und alberne Vöglein dienen nicht an diesem Ort, da viel Gold, Sammet, Seiden, Wehr, Harnisch, Sperber, Kautzen und Blaufüß sind, halt dich zum Roßstall, da man den Hafer schwingt, oder wo man drischet, so kann dirs Glück mit gutem Fried auch dein täglich Körnlein bescheeren.“
sentences.l: “Sparrow and silly little birds are not suited to this place, where there is much gold, velvet, silks, arms, armour, sparrow-hawks, owls and falcons; keep to the horse-stable, where the oats are winnowed, or where one threshes, so fortune may with good peace bestow on you your daily little grain too.”
sentences.i: “A sparrow and foolish little birds have no business in such a place, where there is gold and velvet and silk, weapons, armour, sparrow-hawks, owls and falcons; keep to the horse-stable, where the oats are tossed, or to the threshing-floor, and then fortune may in good peace grant you your daily grain as well.”
sentences.n: “dienen … an diesem Ort” = to be suited to, serve at this place. “Blaufüß” (blue-feet) is the falcon; “Kautzen” = Käuze, owls. “drischet” = drischt, threshes (1857); “bescheeren” = bescheren, to bestow, grant.

sentences.t: „Ja, Vater,“ sagte dieser Sohn, „wenn aber die Stalljungen Hebritzen machen und ihre Maschen und Schlingen ins Stroh binden, da bleibt auch mancher behenken.“
sentences.l: “Yes, father,” said this son, “but when the stable-boys make snares and tie their meshes and nooses in the straw, there many a one gets hung up too.”
sentences.i: “Yes, father,” said this son, “but when the stable-boys set snares and tie their meshes and nooses into the straw, then many a bird is caught fast there too.”
sentences.n: “Hebritzen” is an obscure dialect word for traps or snares; its exact form is uncertain, but the sense is clear from “Maschen und Schlingen” (meshes and nooses). “behenken bleiben” = hängen bleiben, to get caught, hung up.

sentences.t: „Wo hast du das gesehen?“ sagte der Alte.
sentences.l: “Where have you seen that?” said the old one.
sentences.n: The father’s set question again, now with “der Alte,” the old one, as speaker.

sentences.t: „Zu Hof, beim Roßbuben.“
sentences.l: “At court, at the horse-boy’s.”
sentences.i: “At court, with the stable-lad.”
sentences.n: “beim Roßbuben” = bei dem Roßbuben, at/with the horse-boy, the groom. “Roß” = steed, horse.

sentences.t: „O, mein Sohn, Hofbuben, böse Buben!
sentences.l: “O, my son — court-boys, wicked boys!
sentences.i: “O my son — court lads, bad lads!
sentences.n: Another clipped proverb, and a jingle: “Hofbuben, böse Buben.” The exclamation runs on into the following sentence.

sentences.t: bist du zu Hof und um die Herren gewesen und hast keine Federn da gelassen, so hast du ziemlich gelernet und wirst dich in der Welt wohl wissen auszureißen, doch siehe dich um und auf; die Wölfe fressen auch oft die gescheidten Hündlein.“
sentences.l: if you have been at court and about the great and have left no feathers there, then you have learned a fair amount, and will know well how to break yourself away in the world; yet look about you and up: the wolves often eat the clever little hounds too.”
sentences.i: if you have been at court and among the great lords and left no feathers there, then you have learned a good deal, and will know how to slip free in the world; but keep looking about and above — the wolves often devour the clever little dogs as well.”
sentences.n: “keine Federn lassen” = to come off unscathed (a bird “leaving no feathers”). “sich ausreißen” = to tear oneself away, get clear. “siehe dich um und auf” = look around and up; “gescheidt” (1857) = gescheit, clever.

sentences.t: Der Vater nimmt den dritten auch vor sich, „wo hast du dein Heil versucht?“
sentences.l: The father takes the third also before him: “where have you tried your fortune?”
sentences.i: The father takes the third one before him too: “where have you tried your luck?”
sentences.n: “jemanden vor sich nehmen” = to take someone before one, take them aside. “sein Heil versuchen” = to try one’s luck, seek one’s fortune.

sentences.t: „Auf den Fahrwegen und Landstraßen hab ich Kübel und Seil eingeworfen und da bisweilen ein Körnlein oder Gräuplein angetroffen.“
sentences.l: “On the cart-roads and highroads I have thrown in bucket and rope, and there now and then come upon a little grain or a little groat.”
sentences.i: “On the cart-tracks and highroads I dropped in at bucket and rope, and there now and then came upon a grain or a little groat.”
sentences.n: This son forages at wayside wells. “Kübel und Seil” = the well’s bucket and rope; “einwerfen” = to throw/drop in. “Gräuplein” = a little Graupe, a hulled grain or groat; “bisweilen” = now and then.

sentences.t: „Dies ist ja,“ sagt der Vater, „eine feine Nahrung, aber merk gleich wohl auf die Schanz und siehe fleißig auf, sonderlich wenn sich einer bücket und einen Stein aufheben will, da ist dir nicht lang zu bleiben.“
sentences.l: “This is indeed,” says the father, “a fine living, but mark the chance well all the same and look diligently out, especially when someone stoops and means to pick up a stone — there it is not for you to stay long.”
sentences.i: “That is indeed a fine living,” says the father, “but watch your chances closely and keep a sharp lookout, especially when a man bends down and means to pick up a stone — then it is no place for you to linger.”
sentences.n: “auf die Schanz merken” — “Schanz(e)” here is chance, opportunity (from French chance); to mind one’s chances, stay alert. “sich bücken” = to bend down; “bücket” = bückt. “da ist dir nicht lang zu bleiben” — a dative-plus-infinitive of necessity, “there is no long staying for you.”

sentences.t: „Wahr ists,“ sagt der Sohn, „wenn aber einer zuvor einen Wand- oder Handstein im Busen oder Tasche trüge?“
sentences.l: “True it is,” says the son, “but what if someone beforehand carried a wall- or hand-stone in his bosom or pocket?”
sentences.i: “True enough,” says the son, “but what if a man already carried a wall- or hand-stone in his bosom or pocket?”
sentences.n: “ists” = ist es. “trüge” is subjunctive (of tragen), “were to carry,” for the hypothetical. A “Handstein” is a stone small enough to throw by hand — the son foresees the danger before the man need stoop.

sentences.t: „Wo hast du dies gesehn?“
sentences.l: “Where have you seen this?”
sentences.n: “gesehn” = gesehen, seen; the clipped -n is common in speech and verse. The father’s set question once more.

sentences.t: „Bei den Bergleuten, lieber Vater, wenn sie ausfahren, führen sie gemeinlich Handsteine bei sich.“
sentences.l: “Among the miners, dear father — when they go out to work, they commonly carry hand-stones with them.”
sentences.i: “Among the miners, dear father — when they go down to work, they usually carry hand-stones on them.”
sentences.n: “Bergleute” = miners; “ausfahren” is the miners’ word for going out and down to the shift. “gemeinlich” = gemeiniglich, commonly, usually.

sentences.t: „Bergleut, Werkleut, anschlägige Leut!
sentences.l: “Miners, workmen — resourceful folk!
sentences.i: “Miners and workmen — crafty folk!
sentences.n: Another jingling proverb, near-rhyming on “-leut, -leut … Leut.” “anschlägig” = resourceful, full of schemes. The line runs on into the next sentence, which opens the father’s speech that the verse then completes.

sentences.t: bist du um Bergburschen gewesen, so hast du etwas gesehen und erfahren.
sentences.l: if you have been about mining-lads, then you have seen and learned something.
sentences.i: if you have been among mining-lads, then you have seen and learned a thing or two.
sentences.n: The verb-first conditional again (“(if) you have been …, then …”). “erfahren” = to come to know, learn by experience. The father’s speech runs on without a pause into the verse that follows.

sentences.t:
Fahr hin und nimm deiner Sachen gleichwohl gut Acht,
Bergbuben haben manchen Sperling mit Kobold umbracht.“
sentences.l:
Go your way, and take good heed of your affairs all the same:
mine-boys have done many a sparrow to death with Kobold.
sentences.i:
Go on your way, but keep good watch over your affairs even so:
mining-lads have killed many a sparrow with Kobold.
sentences.n: A rhymed couplet — the German rhymes “Acht” / “umbracht.” Lectorium’s rendering does not reproduce the rhyme. “umbracht” = umgebracht, killed. “mit Kobold” is obscure: “Kobold” is the goblin, but in miners’ speech it also named a treacherous ore or the noxious mine-gas that kills — the line probably means the birds died of the mine’s poisonous air. The exact sense is uncertain. “deiner Sachen Acht” — “Acht haben” governs the genitive, heed of your affairs.

sentences.t: Endlich kommt der Vater an jüngsten Sohn.
sentences.l: At last the father comes to the youngest son.
sentences.n: “an jüngsten Sohn” = an den jüngsten Sohn, to the youngest son — the article is dropped, as often in this brisk telling.

sentences.t: „du, mein liebes Gackennestle, du warst allzeit der alberst und schwächest, bleib du bei mir, die Welt hat viel grober und böser Vögel, die krumme Schnäbel und lange Krallen haben und nur auf arme Vöglein lauern und sie verschlucken: halt dich zu deinesgleichen und lies die Spinnlein und Räuplein von den Bäumen oder Häuslein, so bleibst du lang zufrieden.“
sentences.l: “you, my dear nest-baby, you were always the silliest and weakest; stay you with me. The world has many coarse and wicked birds that have crooked beaks and long claws and only lie in wait for poor little birds and swallow them up: keep to your own kind and pick the little spiders and caterpillars off the trees or the little houses, so you will stay content long.”
sentences.i: “you, my dear little nestling, you were always the simplest and weakest — stay here with me. The world is full of coarse, wicked birds with crooked beaks and long claws that lie in wait for poor little birds and gulp them down: keep to your own kind, and pick the little spiders and caterpillars off the trees and the eaves, and you will long stay content.”
sentences.n: “Gackennestle” is a tender coinage — roughly “little cackle-nestling,” the last-hatched darling, a Swabian-flavoured diminutive. “alberst” and “schwächest” = albertste, schwächste, silliest, weakest. “sich halten zu” = to keep to; “Häuslein” here = little houses, birdhouses or eaves.

sentences.t: „Du, mein lieber Vater, wer sich nährt ohn andrer Leut Schaden, der kommt lang hin, und kein Sperber, Habicht, Aar oder Weih wird ihm nicht schaden, wenn er zumal sich und seine ehrliche Nahrung dem lieben Gott all Abend und Morgen treulich befiehlt, welcher aller Wald- und Dorfvöglein Schöpfer und Erhalter ist, der auch der jungen Räblein Geschrei und Gebet höret, denn ohne seinen Willen fällt auch kein Sperling oder Schneekünglein auf die Erde.“
sentences.l: “You, my dear father, whoever feeds himself without other people’s harm gets far, and no sparrow-hawk, goshawk, eagle or kite will do him harm, if he but faithfully commends himself and his honest food to dear God every evening and morning — who is the Creator and Sustainer of all wood- and village-birds, who hears too the young ravens’ crying and prayer; for without his will not even a sparrow or a little snow-king falls to the earth.”
sentences.i: “You, my dear father — whoever feeds himself without doing harm to others gets far, and no sparrow-hawk, goshawk, eagle or kite will harm him, so long as he faithfully commends himself and his honest food to dear God every evening and morning — He who is the Creator and Sustainer of all the birds of wood and village, who hears even the young ravens’ crying and prayer; for without His will not even a sparrow or a little wren falls to the ground.”
sentences.n: The pious son answers in scriptural cadence (cf. the sparrow that does not fall without God’s will). “ohn” = ohne, without; “andrer Leut Schaden” = anderer Leute Schaden, other people’s harm (genitive). The double negative “wird … nicht schaden” is emphatic, not cancelling. “Aar” = eagle (poetic), “Weih” = kite; “Schneekünglein” (little snow-king) is a name for the wren; “Räblein” = little ravens.

sentences.t: „Wo hast du dies gelernt?“
sentences.l: “Where have you learned this?”
sentences.n: The father’s set question a last time — the same probe he put to each brother.

sentences.t: Antwortet der Sohn „wie mich der große Windbraus von dir wegriß, kam ich in eine Kirche, da las ich den Sommer die Fliegen und Spinnen von den Fenstern ab und hörte diese Sprüch predigen, da hat mich der Vater aller Sperlinge den Sommer über ernährt und behütet vor allem Unglück und grimmigen Vögeln.“
sentences.l: The son answers, “when the great gust of wind tore me from you, I came into a church; there I picked the flies and spiders off the windows all summer and heard these sayings preached; there the Father of all sparrows fed me the summer through and guarded me from all misfortune and fierce birds.”
sentences.i: The son answers, “when the great gust of wind tore me away from you, I came into a church; there I picked the flies and spiders off the windows all summer and heard these sayings preached, and there the Father of all sparrows fed me all summer long and kept me from every misfortune and from the fierce birds.”
sentences.n: “wie” here = als, when (temporal), not “how.” “abliesen” (lese … ab) = to pick off; “Sprüch” = Sprüche, sayings, scripture-verses. “der Vater aller Sperlinge” deliberately echoes “the Father of all,” God.

sentences.t: „Traun! mein lieber Sohn, fleuchst du in die Kirchen und hilfest Spinnen und die sumsenden Fliegen aufräumen und zirpst zu Gott wie die jungen Räblein und befiehlst dich dem ewigen Schöpfer, so wirst du wohl bleiben, und wenn die ganze Welt voll wilder tückischer Vögel wäre.
sentences.l: “Truly! my dear son, if you flee into the churches and help clear away spiders and the buzzing flies, and chirp to God like the young ravens, and commend yourself to the eternal Creator, then you will surely be safe, even if the whole world were full of wild, malicious birds.
sentences.i: “Truly, my dear son — if you take flight into the churches and help clear away the spiders and the buzzing flies, and chirp to God like the young ravens, and commend yourself to the eternal Creator, then you will surely come through, even were the whole world full of wild and spiteful birds.
sentences.n: “Traun!” is an old asseveration, “truly, indeed.” “fleuchst” = fliehst/fliegst, an archaic form (of fliehen/fliegen), you flee/fly; “hilfest” = hilfst. “sumsen” = summen, to buzz. “wohl bleiben” = to remain safe. The father’s speech runs on into the closing verse.

sentences.t:
Denn wer dem Herrn befiehlt seine Sach,
schweigt, leidet, wartet, betet, braucht Glimpf, thut gemach,
bewahrt Glaub und gut Gewissen rein,
dem will Gott Schutz und Helfer sein.“
sentences.l:
For whoever commends his cause to the Lord,
keeps silent, suffers, waits, prays, uses gentleness, goes softly,
keeps faith and a good conscience pure,
to him God will be shield and helper.
sentences.i:
For whoever commends his cause to the Lord —
is silent, endures, waits, prays, deals gently, goes quietly,
keeps his faith and a good conscience clean —
to him God will be a shield and a helper.
sentences.n: A four-line rhymed prayer: the German rhymes in couplets, “Sach” / “gemach” and “rein” / “sein.” Lectorium does not reproduce the rhyme. “braucht Glimpf” = uses forbearance, gentleness; “thut gemach” = tut gemach, goes gently, takes it easy (1857 “thut”). “dem will Gott … sein” — the fronted dative “dem” (to him) answers the opening “wer,” whoever.

glossary.sach: die Sache — cause, matter, affair (shortened Sach; seine Sach = his cause)
glossary.weih: der Weih — kite, a bird of prey (= die Weihe; NOT weh/woe)
